title: Educational Technology
summary: Learn to use technology for real learning gains: purposeful use and the SAMR model, low-tech and offline options, digital tools and data, multimedia lesson design, AI in education and digital citizenship.
audience: Teachers, lecturers, trainers, school leaders and education students

body.p: Educational technology (EdTech) is any technology used to support teaching and learning: radio and TV lessons, phones, computers, learning platforms, interactive whiteboards, simulations and AI tools. Technology helps only when it serves a clear learning goal; devices alone do not improve learning.

list: Substitution: technology replaces a tool with no change, such as typing instead of writing.
Augmentation: a small improvement, such as spell-check or instant quiz feedback.
Modification: the task is significantly redesigned, such as collaborative online editing with comments.
Redefinition: new tasks that were not possible before, such as learners recording interviews with community members and publishing a podcast.

body.p: Higher levels are not always better; substitution is fine when it saves time. The key question is: what does this tool let learners do or understand that they could not before?

body.tip: Before adopting a tool, write one sentence: "This tool helps my learners to … , which they struggle with now because …".

body.p: Many learners have limited access to devices, electricity and affordable data. Good EdTech planning starts with what learners actually have.

list: Radio and TV lessons reach large numbers cheaply and were vital during school closures.
Basic phones support SMS quizzes, reminders and interactive voice lessons.
Smartphones are often shared within families; design short, mobile-friendly activities.
Offline content: download materials once at school and use them without connectivity, or use offline servers and memory cards.
Printed materials remain essential alongside digital ones.

body.p: Video is expensive in data. If a lesson video uses about 5 MB per minute at low quality and about 25 MB per minute at higher quality, a 12-minute video uses 60 MB or 300 MB. For a class of 40 that is about 2.4 GB versus 12 GB. Offer low-quality or audio-only versions, transcripts, and zero-rated platforms where available.

body.tip: Ask learners how they access the internet before assigning online work; assumptions widen inequality.

lessons.title: Digital tools for teaching and learning

body.p: A small set of well-used tools beats many half-used ones.

list: Learning management systems (such as Google Classroom, Moodle or Microsoft Teams) organise materials, assignments and feedback.
Quiz tools give instant feedback and show which questions most learners got wrong.
Collaborative documents and whiteboards let learners work together and see each other's thinking.
Simulations and virtual labs let learners experiment safely, for example with circuits or chemical reactions.
Video and screen-recording tools let teachers create short explanations learners can replay.
Messaging groups support communication with learners and parents, with clear rules on times and tone.

body.p: Platforms produce data on completion and scores. If 30 of 40 learners complete an online task (75%), follow up with the 10 who did not: is it access, understanding or motivation? Data should prompt conversations, not replace them.

body.tip: Choose one platform for your class and use it consistently; switching tools often confuses learners and parents.

body.p: Research on multimedia learning offers practical principles for digital materials:

list: Keep videos short and focused, often under about 6 to 10 minutes, one main idea each.
Combine words and relevant pictures, but avoid decorative images that distract.
Narrate diagrams rather than filling the screen with text the narrator reads aloud.
Signal key points with highlighting and headings.
Break content into segments with pauses or questions.
Use a conversational, friendly tone.

body.p: Watching is not learning on its own. Add retrieval questions after each segment, short practice tasks with feedback, discussion prompts and opportunities to apply ideas. Blended learning combines online preparation (such as watching a short video) with active work in class (the flipped classroom).

Add captions to videos, alternative text to images and good contrast to slides; use readable fonts and allow learners to adjust speed. These help learners with disabilities and everyone using a small phone screen.

body.tip: Watch your own digital lesson on a phone with the sound off; if it still makes sense, it is well designed.

body.p: AI tools can generate explanations, practice questions, feedback, translations and lesson ideas, and can act as tutors that answer questions at any time. Used well, they save teachers time and support learners; used badly, they enable shortcuts that skip learning.

list: Teachers: drafting differentiated questions, rubrics and examples, then checking and editing them.
Learners: asking for explanations in simpler words, getting feedback on drafts, practising with quizzes.
Accessibility: text-to-speech, translation and summarising long texts.
AI can produce confident but wrong answers; always verify facts.
Learners must still do the thinking: set tasks that require personal reflection, local data, process evidence or in-class work.
Protect privacy: do not enter learners' personal information into tools without approval.
Watch for bias in generated content.
Follow your school's or ministry's policy on AI use and academic honesty.

body.tip: Teach learners to use AI like a tutor ("explain, then quiz me") rather than like an answer machine.

body.p: Learners need to use technology safely, responsibly and critically.

list: Online safety: strong passwords, privacy settings, not sharing personal information, and recognising scams.
Respectful behaviour: no cyberbullying; know how to report abuse and support those targeted.
Information literacy: check sources, recognise misinformation and edited images.
Digital footprint: posts can be permanent and visible to future employers and universities.
Wellbeing: balance screen time with sleep, exercise and offline relationships.

body.p: Schools need clear acceptable-use policies, safeguarding procedures for online communication between staff and learners, data-protection practices that comply with laws such as POPIA, and plans for maintaining, charging and securing devices. Train teachers as well as learners; confident teachers use technology more effectively.

body.tip: Model the behaviour you expect: credit sources, check facts and communicate respectfully online.

quiz.q: In SAMR, a new task that was impossible before is:
Typing instead of handwriting with no other change is:
Which reaches many learners with no internet?
A 12-minute video at 25 MB per minute uses about:
For a class of 40, the low-quality (60 MB) version totals about:
30 of 40 learners complete a task. Completion is:

options: Fill slides with text and read it aloud
Learners prepare online, then do active work in class
Deaf learners and anyone watching without sound

quiz.q: A key risk of AI tools is that they:
options: Can give confident but wrong answers

quiz.q: Which is a good learner use of AI?
options: Submitting its essay as your own
Asking it to explain a concept and then quiz you
The lasting trail of what you post and do online
